  2806  7. Section 351.907--Reconsideration of an Initial Decision
  2807      Revised Sec.  351.907 establishes the process for reconsideration 
  2808  of an initial decision.
  2809      Paragraph (a) authorizes OPM, in its sole discretion, to reopen and 
  2810  reconsider an initial decision upon request of either party or on OPM's 
  2811  own initiative. An employee, the employee's representative, or the 
  2812  agency may request reconsideration within 30 calendar days from 
  2813  issuance of the initial decision. The request must be filed in the same 
  2814  manner as an initial appeal.
  2815      Paragraph (b) identifies the grounds on which OPM may grant 
  2816  reconsideration. OPM may grant reconsideration if the initial decision 
  2817  contains erroneous findings of material fact sufficient to warrant a 
  2818  different outcome; if the initial decision is based on an erroneous 
  2819  interpretation of statute or regulation or an erroneous application of 
  2820  law to the facts; if new and material evidence or legal argument is 
  2821  available that, despite the party's due diligence, was not available 
  2822  when the record closed; or if OPM finds good cause to reconsider the 
  2823  appeal.
  2824      When a party alleges legal error, the party must explain how the 
  2825  error affected the outcome of the case. For new evidence, the relevant 
  2826  question is whether the information contained in the documents, not 
  2827  merely the documents themselves, was unavailable despite due diligence 
  2828  when the record closed.
  2829      Paragraph (c) describes OPM's authority in a reopened or reviewed 
  2830  case. OPM may issue a reopened and reconsidered decision that affirms, 
  2831  reverses, modifies, vacates, or otherwise decides the case in whole or 
  2832  in part. OPM may require the parties to submit argument and evidence, 
  2833  take any other action necessary for final disposition of the case, and 
  2834  issue an order with a date for compliance.
  2835      Paragraph (d) provides that there is no further right of 
  2836  administrative appeal from the reopened and reconsidered decision.
  2837  8. Section 351.908--Review by the OPM Director
  2838      Section 351.908 reserves to the OPM Director the authority, in the 
  2839  Director's discretion and sua sponte, to reopen and reconsider any 
  2840  appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not yet become 
  2841  final. Once a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909, Sec.  351.908 
  2842  does not provide a separate mechanism for reopening that decision.
  2843      Many commenters (including 0177, 0395, 0411, 0555, 1020, and 
  2844  others) objected to providing the OPM Director with the authority to 
  2845  reopen and reconsider decisions at his or her direction, sua sponte, 
  2846  contending that it violated due process.
  2847      In response to comments expressing concern that Director review 
  2848  could be too open-ended or could undermine the perceived neutrality of 
  2849  OPM adjudication, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify 
  2850  nonexclusive considerations that may inform the Director's decision to 
  2851  reopen and reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision. Under the final 
  2852  rule, the Director may act on the Director's own initiative and only 
  2853  before a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. In determining 
  2854  whether to exercise that authority, the Director may consider, among 
  2855  other things, whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on 
  2856  an erroneous finding of material fact, involves an issue of exceptional 
  2857  importance, affects the governmentwide administration of civil service 
  2858  laws, rules, regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM 
  2859  decision, or otherwise warrants Director review.
  2860      This revision responds to commenters who objected to Director 
  2861  review as insufficiently cabined, while preserving final agency 
  2862  supervision over important legal, factual, policy, consistency, and 
  2863  governmentwide civil service issues. OPM has retained sua sponte 
  2864  Director review because final agency oversight promotes decisional 
  2865  consistency and accountability within OPM's adjudicatory process. The 
  2866  revision does not create a separate right for parties to request 
  2867  Director review; parties may seek reconsideration under Sec.  351.907. 
  2868  If the Director reopens and reconsiders a decision under Sec.  351.908, 
  2869  the Director may take any action available under Sec.  351.907(c). This 
  2870  structure preserves meaningful principal-officer oversight while 
  2871  clarifying that Director review will occur within the rule's record-
  2872  based adjudicatory framework, including the final rule's agency-record, 
  2873  separation-of-functions, ex parte, reconsideration, and finality 
  2874  provisions.
  2875      OPM declines to eliminate Director review entirely. Director review 
  2876  serves both administrative and constitutional functions. As an 
  2877  administrative matter, it ensures that OPM can correct material legal, 
  2878  factual, or procedural errors before a decision becomes final; resolve 
  2879  recurring or important questions of interpretation; and promote uniform 
  2880  application of part 351 across agencies. That review function is 
  2881  especially important in a governmentwide personnel system, where 
  2882  inconsistent interpretations by subordinate adjudicators could produce 
  2883  uneven appeal rights for similarly situated employees in different 
  2884  agencies. Cf. 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), (5) (vesting the OPM Director 
  2885  with responsibility for securing ``accuracy, uniformity, and justice'' 
  2886  in OPM's functions, directing and supervising OPM employees, and 
  2887  executing, administering, and enforcing civil-service laws and 
  2888  regulations).
  2889      Director review also reinforces the rule's consistency with the 
  2890  Appointments Clause. The Constitution requires principal officers to be 
  2891  appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, 
  2892  while Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the 
  2893  President alone, courts of law, or heads of departments. U.S. Const. 
  2894  art. II, Sec.  2, cl. 2. The OPM Director is a presidentially 
  2895  appointed, Senate-confirmed officer. 5 U.S.C. 1102(a). Under the 
  2896  Supreme Court's Appointments Clause precedents, inferior officers must 
  2897  remain subject to direction and supervision by a properly appointed 
  2898  superior officer. Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663-65 (1997). 
  2899  In the adjudicatory context, the Court has treated the availability of 
  2900  review by a superior executive officer as a significant feature 
  2901  distinguishing inferior officers from principal officers. Id. at 665.
  2902      That principle is particularly relevant where subordinate 
  2903  adjudicators exercise significant authority under Federal law. The 
  2904  Supreme Court has held that officials who occupy continuing offices and 
  2905  exercise significant discretion in conducting adjudications may be 
  2906  ``Officers of the United States'' rather than mere employees. See 
  2907  Freytag v. Comm'r, 501 U.S. 868, 881-82 (1991); Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 
  2908  237, 245-51 (2018). The rule preserves supervision by the Director, a 
  2909  principal officer, before OPM's decision becomes final. Consistent with 
  2910  Freytag, Lucia, and related precedents, the Director will appoint, or 
  2911  ratify the appointments of, the OPM personnel assigned to adjudicate 
  2912  appeals under this subpart, ensuring that any adjudicator who exercises 
  2913  significant authority as an inferior officer has been properly 
  2914  appointed.
  2915      The Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Arthrex, 594 U.S. 
  2916  1, 22-23 (2021), confirms the importance of that structure. There, the 
  2917  Court held that administrative patent judges could not constitutionally 
  2918  issue unreviewable final decisions on behalf of the Executive Branch 
  2919  while being appointed only as inferior officers. The constitutional 
  2920  problem was not that subordinate adjudicators participated in deciding 
  2921  cases; it was that their decisions were insulated from review by
  2922  
  2923  [[Page 49253]]
  2924  
  2925  a principal officer. Id. at 25-26. The Court's remedy was to permit 
  2926  discretionary review by the Director of the Patent and Trademark 
  2927  Office, explaining that the Director need not review every decision, 
  2928  but must have authority to review decisions if he chooses. Id. at 27-
  2929  28.
  2930      The appeals process established in this rule follows that model. 
  2931  OPM adjudicators may issue initial decisions, and OPM may reopen and 
  2932  reconsider those decisions on party request or on its own initiative. 
  2933  In addition, the Director may, in his or her discretion, reopen and 
  2934  reconsider any appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not 
  2935  yet become final, and a decision issued by the Director is the final 
  2936  decision of OPM. This structure ensures that no subordinate adjudicator 
  2937  has unreviewable authority to bind OPM or the Executive Branch in an 
  2938  appeal under subpart I of part 351.
  2939      OPM does not agree that the possibility of Director review 
  2940  establishes bias or a due-process violation. Agency heads commonly 
  2941  retain final decisional authority within administrative adjudication 
  2942  systems, and the mere availability of final agency review does not show 
  2943  prejudgment, bad faith, or inability to decide a matter fairly.\33\ The 
  2944  Director's review authority applies only before a decision becomes 
  2945  final. It does not permit adjudication outside the regulatory 
  2946  framework, and it does not eliminate the requirement that decisions be 
  2947  based on the record and the governing standards in part 351. In 
  2948  addition, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify nonexclusive 
  2949  considerations that may inform the Director's decision to reopen and 
  2950  reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision, including whether the 
  2951  decision contains clear legal error, rests on an erroneous finding of 
  2952  material fact, involves an issue of exceptional importance, affects the 
  2953  governmentwide administration of civil service laws, rules, 
  2954  regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM decision, or 
  2955  otherwise warrants Director review.
  2956  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2957  
  2958      \33\ See Fogo de Chao (Holdings) Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland 
  2959  Sec., 769 F.3d 1127, 1148-49 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (declining to find a 
  2960  due process violation where plaintiff did not establish that the 
  2961  individual agency decisionmaker ``ha[d] a closed mind'' and was 
  2962  ``impervious to evidence or argument''); Riggins v. Goodman, 572 
  2963  F.3d 1101, 1115 (10th Cir. 2009) (denying claim of due process 
  2964  violation absent evidence that administrative adjudicators had a 
  2965  pecuniary interest in the case or personal animosity against a 
  2966  party).
  2967  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2968  
  2969      The final rule thus ensures that Director review occurs within a 
  2970  structured adjudicatory process that includes record-based decision-
  2971  making, separation-of-functions protections, ex parte safeguards, 
  2972  reconsideration, and public availability of final merits decisions. 
  2973  Commenters did not identify specific evidence that the OPM Director 
  2974  would prejudge individual RIF appeals or direct outcomes contrary to 
  2975  the record. OPM therefore declines to eliminate Director review.
  2976  9. Section 351.909--Final Decision
  2977      Revised Sec.  351.909 explains when decisions issued under subpart 
  2978  I become final and the effect of finality.
  2979      Paragraph (a) provides that an initial decision becomes OPM's final 
  2980  decision 30 calendar days after issuance unless, before that time, a 
  2981  party timely requests reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 
  2982  or the Director reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908.
  2983      Paragraph (b) provides that a timely request for reconsideration 
  2984  under Sec.  351.907 suspends finality. If OPM denies or dismisses the 
  2985  request without reopening the initial decision, the initial decision 
  2986  becomes OPM's final decision 30 calendar days after issuance of the

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

  1742  H. Scope of RIF Appeals and Collateral Claims
  1743  
  1744      Commenters 0370, 0928, 0962, 1025, 1089, 1092, 1099, 1165, and 1217 
  1745  raised concerns about the scope of OPM review and the preservation of 
  1746  collateral claims. Commenters argued that the proposal could weaken 
  1747  civil-rights enforcement, eliminate mixed-case processing, prevent 
  1748  employees from raising pretext or retaliation, or force employees into 
  1749  multiple forums. Commenters 0046, 0074, 0540, and 1252 contended that 
  1750  the rule would eliminate the ability to appeal discrimination claims in 
  1751  connection with RIFs entirely and allow agencies to RIF employees in 
  1752  protected classes with impunity.
  1753      The final rule clarifies the scope of OPM's review. OPM will 
  1754  adjudicate whether the agency failed to comply with an applicable 
  1755  statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 351 and 
  1756  whether that failure prejudiced the appellant. This includes RIF-
  1757  compliance issues such as coverage, competitive area, competitive 
  1758  level, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, notice, 
  1759  special RIF circumstances, and related requirements.
  1760      At the same time, the final rule preserves collateral statutory 
  1761  avenues. Final Sec.  351.901(c) states that the procedures in part 351 
  1762  are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action, but do not 
  1763  otherwise preclude an employee from filing a complaint, appeal, or 
  1764  other matter within the jurisdiction of EEOC, an Inspector General, 
  1765  MSPB, DOL VETS, or OSC. This provision reflects OPM's intent to channel 
  1766  direct challenges to RIF compliance through OPM while preserving 
  1767  matters Congress or applicable law has assigned to other forums.
  1768      OPM acknowledges that some claims previously could have been 
  1769  combined with a RIF appeal before MSPB because OPM's regulation made 
  1770  RIF actions appealable to MSPB. That prior combined forum was a 
  1771  consequence of OPM's regulatory delegation to MSPB, not an independent 
  1772  statutory requirement that OPM retain MSPB jurisdiction. The final rule 
  1773  preserves the substantive availability of discrimination, 
  1774  whistleblower, veterans' rights, prohibited-personnel-practice, and 
  1775  Inspector General matters in the proper forums.
  1776      Commenter 0463 asserted that the exclusive RIF appeal procedure 
  1777  could abrogate or supersede appeal rights available to preference 
  1778  eligible veterans under 5 U.S.C. 3330a and 3330b. OPM disagrees. The 
  1779  final rule's exclusivity provision governs direct appeals of RIF 
  1780  actions under part 351; it does not displace independent statutory 
  1781  causes of action that Congress assigned to other forums. Final Sec.  
  1782  351.901(c) expressly preserves an employee's ability to file a 
  1783  complaint, appeal, or other matter within the jurisdiction of, among 
  1784  others, MSPB and the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment and 
  1785  Training Service. That preservation language includes claims under the 
  1786  Veterans Employment Opportunities Act. Under 5 U.S.C. 3330a, a 
  1787  preference eligible who alleges that an agency violated the 
  1788  individual's rights under a statute or regulation relating to veterans' 
  1789  preference may file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, and, if 
  1790  the matter is not resolved, may appeal to MSPB under the procedures 
  1791  Congress specified. 5 U.S.C. 3330a. Section 3330b separately provides 
  1792  for judicial redress in district court in lieu of continuing the 
  1793  administrative redress procedure after the statutory prerequisites are 
  1794  met. 5 U.S.C. 3330b. Nothing in this final rule alters those statutory 
  1795  rights, filing deadlines, forum assignments, or judicial-redress 
  1796  provisions.
  1797      The final rule also reinforces, rather than weakens, the ability to 
  1798  identify and address veterans' preference issues in a RIF appeal. 
  1799  Section 351.903(b) requires the agency record to include documents 
  1800  establishing the appellant's veterans' preference status and related 
  1801  retention information, including records supporting veterans' 
  1802  preference credit, tenure subgroup, service computation date, the 
  1803  retention register, order of release, assignment rights, and any 
  1804  special RIF circumstance relevant to the appellant. Thus, where the 
  1805  issue is whether the agency complied with part 351's RIF requirements 
  1806  as applied to a preference eligible, OPM will have the relevant RIF 
  1807  record before it. Where the issue is an independent veterans' 
  1808  preference claim under 5 U.S.C. 3330a
  1809  
  1810  [[Page 49244]]
  1811  
  1812  or 3330b, the final rule leaves that statutory route undisturbed.
  1813      Commenter 0074 similarly asserted that the revised RIF appeal 
  1814  procedure would allow agencies to engage in pretextual terminations of 
  1815  employees with disabilities in violation of the Rehabilitation Act of 
  1816  1973. OPM disagrees. The final rule does not authorize agencies to use 
  1817  RIF procedures as a pretext for disability discrimination or any other 
  1818  unlawful personnel practice. Federal employees and applicants remain 
  1819  protected by section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. 791, and 
  1820  the remedies, procedures, and rights available under 29 U.S.C. 794a, 
  1821  including the Federal-sector procedures incorporated from Title VII. In 
  1822  addition, disability discrimination remains a prohibited personnel 
  1823  practice under 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(1)(D). The final rule expressly 
  1824  preserves matters within the jurisdiction of the EEOC and OSC and 
  1825  therefore does not redirect Rehabilitation Act claims into OPM's RIF 
  1826  appeal process or limit the remedies available under those statutes.
  1827  
  1828  I. Collective Bargaining, Grievance Arbitration, and CBAs
  1829  
  1830      Commenters 0962, 1025, 1092, 0928, and 1217 objected to the 
  1831  proposal's treatment of negotiated grievance procedures, arbitration, 
  1832  and collective bargaining agreements. These commenters argued that the 
  1833  Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute protects negotiated 
  1834  grievance and arbitration procedures; that RIF matters are not among 
  1835  the matters excluded from negotiated grievance procedures under 5 
  1836  U.S.C. 7121(c); that questions of arbitrability should be resolved 
  1837  through negotiated grievance procedures; and that OPM may not use a 
  1838  governmentwide regulation to eliminate existing collective-bargaining 
  1839  rights or union representation. Other commenters, including 0221, 0584, 
  1840  0587, 0591, and 0621, asserted that the proposal would unlawfully 
  1841  supersede existing CBAs, while commenters 0386 and 1004 requested a 
  1842  clearer legal basis for OPM's position. Commenters 0049, 0092, 0483, 
  1843  and others objected as a policy matter to any prospective limitation on 
  1844  negotiated RIF appeal procedures.
  1845      OPM has considered these comments and has decided to finalize the 
  1846  regulatory text as initially proposed, with some modifications. The 
  1847  final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  1848  ``sole and exclusive means'' of appealing a RIF action, and matters 
  1849  relating to such actions may not be raised under a negotiated grievance 
  1850  procedure or contested through grievance arbitration, but employees are 
  1851  not otherwise impeded from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter 
  1852  within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, an Inspector General, MSPB, DOL 
  1853  VETS, or OSC.
  1854      OPM continues to conclude that a single governmentwide process for 
  1855  direct RIF-compliance appeals is necessary to ensure uniform 
  1856  interpretation and application of part 351. RIF appeals under part 351 
  1857  involve governmentwide rules governing competitive areas, competitive 
  1858  levels, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, 
  1859  notice, and related requirements. Allowing agencies to create or 
  1860  bargain for parallel direct appeal mechanisms for the same RIF-
  1861  compliance claim would undermine the consistency, finality, and 
  1862  efficiency the final rule is designed to achieve.
  1863      This conclusion is consistent with 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). That 
  1864  provision states that the duty to bargain extends only ``to the extent 
  1865  not inconsistent with any Federal law or any governmentwide rule or 
  1866  regulation,'' and, for matters that are the subject of a rule or 
  1867  regulation, applies only where the rule or regulation is not 
  1868  governmentwide. 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). This final rule is a 
  1869  governmentwide regulation: it applies across agencies to appeals of 
  1870  covered RIF actions under part 351. To that end, it firmly and 
  1871  completely limits the flexibility of agencies to provide processes not 
  1872  contemplated by this rule, including grievance arbitration. See U.S. 
  1873  Dep't of Treasury, I.R.S. v. FLRA, 996 F.2d 1246, 1250 (D.C. Cir. 1993) 
  1874  (IRS) (5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) ``permits the government to pull a subject 
  1875  out of the bargaining process by issuing a governmentwide rule that 
  1876  creates a regime inconsistent with bargaining,'' including where a 
  1877  regulation ``sets out an exclusive method of resolving any claims''). 
  1878  Accordingly, agencies may not bargain for a claims-channeling process 
  1879  that conflicts with the final rule's designation of part 351 as the 
  1880  sole and exclusive means of directly appealing a RIF action.
  1881      OPM is not persuaded by commenters' argument that 5 U.S.C. 
  1882  7121(a)(1) overrides this conclusion. Section 7121(a)(1) requires CBAs 
  1883  to provide procedures for settlement of grievances, including questions 
  1884  of arbitrability, and makes those procedures the exclusive 
  1885  administrative procedures for grievances that fall within their 
  1886  coverage. But that provision must be read together with section 
  1887  7117(a)(1), which limits the duty to bargain where the matter is 
  1888  inconsistent with Federal law or a governmentwide rule or regulation. 
  1889  The broad definition of ``grievance'' in 5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(9) likewise 
  1890  does not displace section 7117(a)(1). The fact that RIFs are not listed 
  1891  in section 7121(c) does not mean parties may bargain for an alternative 
  1892  direct RIF appeal procedure that conflicts with a governmentwide 
  1893  regulation establishing a single appeal process.
  1894      The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeal's decision in IRS addressed 
  1895  exactly this issue. The court held that a union proposal that would 
  1896  permit grievances over contracting out was non-negotiable as it 
  1897  conflicted with OMB Circular A-76, a government-wide rule that 
  1898  prescribed the exclusive method for resolving disputes over contracting 
  1899  decisions. The court thus held that Circular A-76 prohibited bargaining 
  1900  over conflicting appeals processes. The final Sec.  351.901(c) 
  1901  similarly prohibits creating an alternative RIF appeals process through 
  1902  collective bargaining.
  1903      OPM also disagrees with Commenter 0962's assertion that section 
  1904  7121(a)(1) has primacy over section 7117(a)(1). Sections 7103, 7117, 
  1905  and 7121 are part of the same statutory scheme and must be read 
  1906  together. Section 7121 establishes negotiated grievance procedures for 
  1907  matters properly within a CBA's coverage; section 7117(a)(1) defines 
  1908  the outer boundary of the bargaining obligation where Federal law or a 
  1909  governmentwide regulation has occupied the field. Reading section 7121 
  1910  to require negotiated grievance arbitration of direct RIF appeals 
  1911  notwithstanding section 7117 would effectively nullify section 
  1912  7117(a)(1) for any matter that could be characterized as a grievance. 
  1913  In IRS the D.C. Circuit expressly rejected that statutory construction. 
  1914  OPM accordingly declines to adopt that reading.
  1915      Nor is this final rule merely a restatement of management rights 
  1916  under 5 U.S.C. 7106. Section 7106 preserves agency authority, subject 
  1917  to subsection (b), to determine mission, budget, organization, number 
  1918  of employees, internal security practices, and to lay off and retain 
  1919  employees, while also preserving bargaining over procedures and 
  1920  appropriate arrangements in appropriate circumstances. 5 U.S.C. 
  1921  7106(a), (b). The final rule does not simply repeat those management 
  1922  rights. It establishes a detailed governmentwide appellate process 
  1923  governing who may appeal, the burden of proof, filing deadlines, 
  1924  agency-record production, service, replies, inspection of the appellate 
  1925  record, representation, adjudication, protective orders, 
  1926  reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  1927  
  1928  [[Page 49245]]
  1929  
  1930      For that reason, commenters' reliance on Office of Personnel 
  1931  Management v. FLRA, 864 F.2d 165 (D.C. Cir. 1988), is misplaced. In 
  1932  that case, the court addressed whether a governmentwide regulation that 
  1933  merely restated management rights could displace bargaining 
  1934  obligations. This rule does not merely restate a management right; it 
  1935  creates a specific, comprehensive appeal procedure for covered RIF 
  1936  actions. The final rule is therefore more closely aligned with the 
  1937  principle that a governmentwide rule may establish an exclusive method 
  1938  for resolving a particular category of claims, rather than simply 
  1939  invoking management rights at a high level of generality.
  1940      OPM also considered comments invoking the general purposes of the 
  1941  FSLMRS, including 5 U.S.C. 7101(a)(1), which recognizes that collective 
  1942  bargaining safeguards the public interest, contributes to the effective 
  1943  conduct of public business, and facilitates amicable dispute 
  1944  resolution. OPM does not dispute those principles. But section 7101 
  1945  must be read with the rest of chapter 71, including section 7117(a)(1), 
  1946  and with section 7101(b)'s direction that chapter 71 be interpreted 
  1947  consistently with the requirements of an effective and efficient 
  1948  Government. Those provisions support, rather than preclude, a 
  1949  governmentwide rule establishing one uniform process for direct RIF-
  1950  compliance appeals and prohibiting grievances over matters pertaining 
  1951  to RIF appeals.
  1952      In addition to the benefits of maintaining a uniform process for 
  1953  direct RIF-compliance appeals, OPM believes it is beneficial to 
  1954  foreclose grievance arbitration in particular as a forum for 
  1955  adjudicating RIF appeals. As OPM explained in the proposed rule, the 
  1956  arbitrators who adjudicate Federal-sector grievances are private 
  1957  contractors who typically do not have a background in agency operations 
  1958  or Federal employment law. This makes them ill-suited to evaluate 
  1959  potentially complex issues involved in arbitration appeals. OPM is 
  1960  aware of multiple studies showing that, across multiple 
  1961  administrations, the FLRA overturns arbitral awards at a high rate.\24\ 
  1962  The author of one of these studies, himself an arbitrator, concluded 
  1963  that ``Federal sector arbitration is more complex than private sector 
  1964  arbitration. The federal field is full of land mines in the form of 
  1965  laws with which federal sector arbitrators may be less familiar.'' \25\ 
  1966  Foreclosing grievance arbitration ensures adjudication will be handled 
  1967  by MSAC employees with specialized legal and subject matter expertise 
  1968  who are less likely to make reversible errors.
  1969  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1970  
  1971      \24\ See James Sherk, ``Federal Union Arbitrators Frequently 
  1972  Misapply the Law,'' (Aug. 2, 2023), https://www.americafirstpolicy.com/issues/expert-insight-federal-union-arbitrators-frequently-misapply-the-law (finding that between 2019 
  1973  and 2023 over 40 percent of arbitration awards were overturned or 
  1974  remanded upon appeal); see also Helburn, B. (2019). The Trump FLRA: 
  1975  Fair or foul (Helburn), at 6. https://cdn.govexec.com/media/gbc/docs/pdfs_edit/060619ew1.pdf (finding the FLRA set aside or remanded 
  1976  arbitration awards 80, 50, and 43 percent of the time in a sampling 
  1977  of cases arising under the Trump 45, Obama, and George W. Bush 
  1978  Administrations, respectively).
  1979      \25\ Helburn at 10.
  1980  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1981  
  1982      Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. 7122(a) arbitral awards concerning RIF 
  1983  appeals are subject to FLRA review. This review can be protracted, 
  1984  especially if the FLRA loses a quorum or the FLRA has a vacancy and the 
  1985  remaining members deadlock.\26\ Authorizing grievance arbitration over 
  1986  RIF actions would thus create a protracted second level of appeals that 
  1987  would undermine the expeditious resolution of cases. OPM declines to 
  1988  adopt this approach.
  1989  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1990  
  1991      \26\ The FLRA has reported that in FY 2024 the average age of 
  1992  pending (not decided) arbitration cases undergoing review was 307 
  1993  days. See U.S. Federal Labor Relations Authority, Congressional 
  1994  Budget Justification 2026, at 19. https://www.flra.gov/system/files/webfm/FLRA%20Agency-wide/Public%20Affairs/CBJ/FLRA%20FY26%20CBJ%20-%20Final.pdf.
  1995  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1996  
  1997      OPM also clarifies that the final rule does not retroactively 
  1998  invalidate existing CBAs or purport to adjudicate particular CBA 
  1999  disputes in this rulemaking. To the extent commenters argued that the 
  2000  proposal would automatically vitiate existing agreements mid-term, OPM 
  2001  does not adopt that position in the final rule. Rather, when agreements 
  2002  are renegotiated, this governmentwide rule will limit agencies' duty 
  2003  and ability to bargain for provisions that create a direct RIF appeal 
  2004  process inconsistent with part 351. Questions concerning the effect of 
  2005  particular existing agreement provisions, negotiability disputes, or 
  2006  unfair-labor-practice allegations remain matters for resolution under 
  2007  chapter 71 by the appropriate forum.
  2008      OPM also disagrees that the final rule eliminates union 
  2009  representation. Final Sec.  351.904(a) provides that an appellant may 
  2010  select a representative of the appellant's choice to assist in 
  2011  preparing and presenting an appeal, provided the appellant submits a 
  2012  written designation of representative for the specific appeal. That 
  2013  representative may be a union representative where otherwise 
  2014  appropriate. Separate limitations on official time, duty status, and 
  2015  reimbursement for Federal employee representatives are addressed in the 
  2016  representation and official-time discussion.
  2017      OPM therefore declines to revise the final rule to permit 
  2018  negotiated grievance arbitration to serve as an alternative direct 
  2019  appeal mechanism for covered RIF actions under part 351. The final rule 
  2020  establishes a uniform OPM process for direct RIF appeals while 
  2021  preserving collateral statutory matters in the forums Congress or 
  2022  applicable law has designated. This approach gives effect to both the 
  2023  RIF appeal framework in part 351 and the limits on bargaining imposed 
  2024  by 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1), while avoiding retroactive invalidation of 
  2025  existing CBAs in this rulemaking.

  3370  B. Regulatory Alternatives
  3371  
  3372      OPM considered several alternatives before adopting the final rule.
  3373      First, OPM considered taking no action and retaining the existing 
  3374  regulatory delegation of RIF appeals to MSPB. OPM rejected that 
  3375  alternative. The current framework separates responsibility for the RIF 
  3376  regulations from responsibility for adjudicating disputes under those 
  3377  regulations. OPM prescribes and interprets the governmentwide RIF 
  3378  rules, while MSPB adjudicates RIF appeals under procedures OPM cannot 
  3379  control. OPM has determined that this divided structure produces 
  3380  unnecessary fragmentation, delay, and cost, and does not best serve 
  3381  employees, agencies, or the public. Retaining the status quo also would 
  3382  not address the concerns that prompted this rulemaking, including the 
  3383  burden of MSPB-style litigation, the need for more consistent 
  3384  interpretation of part 351, and the need for a process better tailored 
  3385  to the record-based issues ordinarily presented in RIF appeals.
  3386      Second, OPM considered eliminating administrative RIF appeals 
  3387  entirely. Congress directed that a RIF notice include a description of 
  3388  any appeal or other rights that ``may be available,'' 5 U.S.C. 
  3389  3502(d)(2)(E), and OPM has discretion to determine the contours of any 
  3390  regulatory RIF appeal procedure for non-SES employees. OPM declined to 
  3391  eliminate administrative RIF appeals. Employees have long had an 
  3392  administrative mechanism to challenge whether a RIF action was 
  3393  conducted consistently with applicable statute and regulation. 
  3394  Eliminating that mechanism would reduce adjudication costs, but it 
  3395  would also remove an orderly process for correcting prejudicial errors 
  3396  in the application of RIF requirements. OPM concluded that employees 
  3397  should continue to have a direct administrative avenue to challenge 
  3398  covered RIF actions, provided the process is structured to resolve RIF-
  3399  compliance issues efficiently and consistently.
  3400      Third, OPM considered delegating RIF appeal adjudication to 
  3401  employing agencies. OPM rejected that alternative because it would 
  3402  create greater risk of inconsistent results and diminished confidence 
  3403  in the neutrality of the process. A decentralized agency-level appeal 
  3404  system would require each agency conducting a RIF to adjudicate direct 
  3405  challenges to its own RIF actions, which would heighten the very 
  3406  impartiality concerns commenters raised. It would also undermine 
  3407  governmentwide consistency in applying part 351 and reduce the 
  3408  efficiency gains expected from a single OPM-administered process.
  3409      Fourth, OPM considered retaining MSPB as the forum while attempting 
  3410  to impose OPM-designed streamlined procedures, including more limited 
  3411  discovery, record-based review, and hearings only where necessary. OPM 
  3412  rejected this alternative because it would not accomplish OPM's 
  3413  objective. In AFGE v. OPM, 821 F.2d 761, 768-69 (D.C. Cir. 1987), the 
  3414  D.C. Circuit explained that where OPM elects to use MSPB as the 
  3415  adjudicative forum, OPM may not dictate MSPB's adjudicatory procedures 
  3416  in the manner OPM had attempted. Thus, recommendations to streamline 
  3417  MSPB procedures, including those advanced by Commenters 0308 and 0386, 
  3418  cannot be implemented by OPM while leaving RIF appeals at MSPB. Several 
  3419  of those procedural concepts are instead reflected in the
  3420  
  3421  [[Page 49257]]
  3422  
  3423  final OPM process, including written-record review, targeted fact 
  3424  development, and hearings when necessary and efficient.
  3425      Fifth, OPM considered moving RIF appeals to OPM while retaining 
  3426  MSPB-style procedures, including broader discovery and a hearing as of 
  3427  right. OPM rejected that alternative because it would preserve many of 
  3428  the features that make the current process costly, lengthy, and poorly 
  3429  suited to many RIF appeals. The final rule is not merely a forum 
  3430  change. Its purpose is to establish a RIF-specific process tailored to 
  3431  the issues ordinarily presented in part 351 appeals: coverage, 
  3432  competitive area, competitive level, retention standing, order of 
  3433  release, assignment rights, notice, and related RIF-compliance 
  3434  requirements. OPM concluded that written-record adjudication, supported 
  3435  by a complete agency record and supplemented by additional procedures 
  3436  when necessary and efficient, better balances fairness, accuracy, 
  3437  speed, and administrative cost.
  3438      Sixth, OPM considered relying on negotiated grievance arbitration 
  3439  or agency-specific appeal procedures as an alternative to a 
  3440  governmentwide OPM appeal process. OPM rejected that approach for 
  3441  direct RIF-compliance appeals. RIF appeals require uniform application 
  3442  of governmentwide regulations, and allowing parallel direct appeal 
  3443  mechanisms across agencies or bargaining units would undermine 
  3444  consistency and finality. Arbitrators also lack the expertise necessary 
  3445  to adjudicate RIF appeals effectively. At the same time, OPM revised 
  3446  the final regulatory text to address comments concerning collateral 
  3447  forums outside of collective bargaining and grievance arbitration. 
  3448  Final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  3449  sole and exclusive means of appealing a covered RIF action, bars 
  3450  raising such actions and matters relating to their appeal under 
  3451  negotiated grievance procedures or through grievance arbitration, and 
  3452  preserves matters within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, Inspectors 
  3453  General, MSPB where it has independent jurisdiction, DOL VETS, and OSC.
  3454      Seventh, OPM considered retaining MSPB review while seeking 
  3455  increased MSPB staffing, specialized MSPB RIF tracks, expedited MSPB 
  3456  procedures, or other MSPB case-management reforms. OPM rejected these 
  3457  alternatives because they depend on institutional, budgetary, or 
  3458  procedural choices outside OPM's control and would not resolve the 
  3459  fundamental fragmentation created by locating adjudication outside the 
  3460  agency responsible for part 351. Additional MSPB resources also would 
  3461  not give OPM authority to require the RIF-specific process OPM has 
  3462  determined is appropriate.
  3463      Commenters 0928, 1092, and 1099 argued that OPM failed to consider 
  3464  less disruptive alternatives, including retaining MSPB review, 
  3465  improving MSPB procedures, creating expedited MSPB tracks, preserving 
  3466  grievance arbitration, or otherwise modifying the existing system. OPM 
  3467  has considered those alternatives and disagrees that they would better 
  3468  accomplish the goals of this rulemaking. Retaining MSPB would preserve 
  3469  the divided structure OPM seeks to correct. Attempting to dictate MSPB 
  3470  procedures would conflict with AFGE v. OPM. Mirroring MSPB procedures 
  3471  at OPM would preserve unnecessary procedural burden. Agency-level 
  3472  adjudication would reduce consistency and raise neutrality concerns. 
  3473  Eliminating appeals entirely would go too far by removing a useful 
  3474  mechanism for correcting prejudicial RIF errors.
  3475      OPM selected the final approach because it best balances fairness, 
  3476  efficiency, consistency, and cost. The final rule preserves an 
  3477  administrative appeal right for employees furloughed for more than 30 
  3478  days, separated, or demoted by a RIF action; clarifies the appellant's 
  3479  burden and prejudice standard; requires the agency to produce the 
  3480  complete RIF-specific agency record to OPM; requires service of the 
  3481  agency record on the appellant subject only to legally required 
  3482  disclosure limits; permits an appellant reply; authorizes additional 
  3483  information, audits, investigations, and hearings when necessary and 
  3484  efficient; provides reconsideration and limited Director review before 
  3485  finality; preserves collateral statutory forums; and authorizes 
  3486  corrective relief where the appellant proves prejudicial RIF error.
  3487      Accordingly, OPM concludes that the selected alternative is 
  3488  preferable to the status quo and to the other alternatives considered. 
  3489  It preserves meaningful administrative review while reducing 
  3490  fragmentation, aligning adjudication with OPM's governmentwide RIF 
  3491  expertise, and establishing procedures better tailored to the nature of 
  3492  RIF appeals.
  3493  
  3494  C. Expected Impact
  3495  
  3496      OPM expects the final rule to produce a more streamlined, 
  3497  consistent, and administrable RIF appeal process. The rule does not 
  3498  alter the substantive requirements agencies must follow when conducting 
  3499  a RIF, nor does it authorize OPM to substitute its judgment for an 
  3500  agency's workforce-management determinations. Rather, it changes the 
  3501  forum and procedures for adjudicating whether an agency complied with 
  3502  applicable statutes and OPM regulations governing RIF actions under 
  3503  part 351 and whether any failure prejudiced the appellant.
  3504      The revised process is designed to match the issues ordinarily 
  3505  presented in RIF appeals. RIF appeals typically turn on the application 
  3506  of established statutory and regulatory criteria to an agency record, 
  3507  including coverage, competitive area, competitive level, retention 
  3508  standing, order of release, assignment rights, notice, and related part 
  3509  351 requirements. These issues generally are well suited to record-
  3510  based adjudication, supplemented where necessary by targeted requests 
  3511  for information, audits, investigations, or hearings when OPM 
  3512  determines that such procedures are necessary and efficient.
  3513      OPM will administer this process through MSAC, an external-facing 
  3514  OPM component with longstanding oversight and adjudicatory 
  3515  responsibilities. MSAC already adjudicates Federal personnel matters, 
  3516  including classification appeals, Fair Labor Standards Act claims, 
  3517  compensation and leave claims, and declination-of-reasonable-offer 
  3518  claims. RIF appeals are well suited to MSAC's institutional role 
  3519  because they require application of OPM's governmentwide personnel 
  3520  regulations to agency records and because MSAC is responsible for 
  3521  evaluating agency compliance with civil service laws, merit system 
  3522  principles, and related regulations.
  3523      The final rule also strengthens the record on which appeals will be 
  3524  decided. The agency must produce the complete agency record to OPM and 
  3525  must serve the appellant with the agency record, subject only to 
  3526  legally required disclosure limitations. The required record includes, 
  3527  as applicable, the RIF notice, effective-date documentation, records 
  3528  supporting the reason for the RIF, coverage and appointment records, 
  3529  competitive-area and competitive-level documentation, retention-
  3530  register materials, order-of-release records, assignment-rights 
  3531  materials, special RIF-circumstance records, and a certification that 
  3532  the complete agency record has been produced. These requirements will 
  3533  allow OPM to adjudicate RIF appeals on a complete and reviewable record 
  3534  while giving appellants meaningful access to the materials needed to 
  3535  test whether the agency complied with part 351.
  3536      For employees, the final rule is expected to provide faster and 
  3537  clearer resolution of RIF appeals while
  3538  
  3539  [[Page 49258]]
  3540  
  3541  preserving meaningful administrative review. An employee who is 
  3542  furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a RIF action 
  3543  may appeal to OPM. The employee may submit supporting documentation, 
  3544  review the agency response, file a reply, inspect OPM's appellate 
  3545  record subject to legal limits, and obtain corrective relief if the 
  3546  employee proves a prejudicial violation of an applicable RIF statute or 
  3547  OPM regulation. Faster resolution benefits employees whether the action 
  3548  is corrected or sustained: if the agency committed a prejudicial error, 
  3549  relief can be ordered sooner; if the action is upheld, the employee 
  3550  receives earlier certainty for purposes of Federal reemployment, non-
  3551  Federal employment, financial planning, and career decisions.
  3552      For agencies, the final rule is expected to reduce litigation 
  3553  burden, improve predictability, and promote finality. Under the prior 
  3554  framework, RIF appeals could proceed through MSPB's multi-stage 
  3555  process, including discovery, hearing preparation, evidentiary 
  3556  hearings, petitions for review, and judicial review where available. 
  3557  That process can require substantial participation by agency counsel, 
  3558  human-resources staff, supervisors, managers, and witnesses. The OPM 
  3559  process preserves the ability to develop the record where necessary but 
  3560  avoids applying the same litigation model to every appeal regardless of 
  3561  whether the issues can be resolved on the written record.
  3562      For OPM, the final rule consolidates interpretation, oversight, and 
  3563  adjudication of part 351 within the agency charged with prescribing and 
  3564  administering governmentwide RIF regulations. This alignment will 
  3565  promote more consistent interpretation of OPM's RIF rules and reduce 
  3566  the fragmentation created when one agency writes and interprets the 
  3567  regulations while another adjudicates appeals under procedures outside 
  3568  OPM's control. OPM expects that MSAC's existing adjudicatory 
  3569  infrastructure and compliance experience will allow OPM to administer 
  3570  RIF appeals efficiently while maintaining record-based decision making 
  3571  and appropriate separation between policy and adjudicatory functions.
  3572      The final rule also includes safeguards designed to support fair 
  3573  and consistent adjudication. OPM adjudicators must be insulated from 
  3574  officials who participated personally and substantially in the 
  3575  challenged personnel action or provided case-specific advice concerning 
  3576  that action. OPM adjudicators may not consider material ex parte 
  3577  communications concerning the merits of an appeal, and any such 
  3578  communication must be summarized in the record with an opportunity for 
  3579  the parties to respond unless disclosure is prohibited by law. OPM may 
  3580  require additional information, conduct an audit or investigation when 
  3581  the existing record is insufficient to resolve a material issue within 
  3582  OPM's jurisdiction, and hold a hearing when necessary and efficient. 
  3583  These safeguards allow OPM to achieve the efficiency benefits of 
  3584  record-based review without eliminating tools needed to resolve 
  3585  material factual or legal issues.
  3586      For MSPB, the rule will remove future part 351 RIF appeals from its 
  3587  docket, except where MSPB has independent statutory jurisdiction over a 
  3588  matter not displaced by this rule. That change will allow MSPB to focus 
  3589  resources on matters Congress made appealable to MSPB by statute, while 
  3590  OPM adjudicates the regulatory RIF appeal right established under part 
  3591  351.
  3592      Overall, OPM expects the final rule to reduce delay, decrease 
  3593  unnecessary litigation costs, improve consistency in the application of 
  3594  part 351, and provide employees and agencies with more timely finality. 
  3595  The rule preserves an administrative appeal mechanism, strengthens the 
  3596  agency-record requirement, allows targeted fact development where 
  3597  needed, and provides corrective relief for prejudicial RIF error. OPM 
  3598  concludes that this structure better serves employees, agencies, and 
  3599  the public than the prior fragmented process.

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a proposed rule to revise its reduction-in-force (RIF) regulations. The proposed rule would make the RIF regulations more streamlined, efficient, and merit-based by prioritizing performance over tenure and length of service when determining which employees will be retained in a RIF and modifying the types of employees who are excluded from RIF competition. OPM also proposes to revise its regulations regarding the reemployment priority list (RPL), career transition assistance program (CTAP), the interagency career transition assistance program (ICTAP), transfers of function, and furloughs.

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).

tools.name: fr_text

Document number:   2026-21320
Title:             Administrative Leave for Workforce Realignment and Other Purposes
Type:              Rule
Action:            Final rule.
Agencies:          Personnel Management Office
Citation:          91 FR 65924
Pages:             65924-65940 (17 pages)
Published:         2026-10-19
Effective:         2026-11-18
Dates:             This rule is effective November 18, 2026.
Docket:            Docket ID: OPM-2026-0397
CFR affected:      5 CFR 351, 5 CFR 630, 5 CFR 715
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Emergency preparedness, Government employees, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Wages, Weather
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/19/2026-21320/administrative-leave-for-workforce-realignment-and-other-purposes
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-19/pdf/2026-21320.pdf

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to amend its regulations governing administrative leave for workforce realignment and other purposes. This final rule more fully addresses the appropriate uses of administrative leave, including use in connection with deferred resignation programs and other workforce realignment initiatives, and for other purposes. The final rule also clarifies when an agency may provide administrative leave during a reduction-in-force notice period and accept or deny an employee's request to withdraw a resignation in the context of a deferred resignation program.

Use `toc`, `grep` or `text` with this document number to read the full text.

Title:             Reduction in Force Appeals
Type:              Rule

Agencies:          Personnel Management Office
Citation:          91 FR 49230

Published:         2026-08-03
Effective:         2026-09-02
Dates:             Effective September 2, 2026. This final rule applies only to a RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026.
Docket:            Docket ID: OPM-2025-0239
RIN:               3206-AO99
Significant:       True
CFR affected:      5 CFR 351
Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Government employees
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/03/2026-15666/reduction-in-force-appeals
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-03/pdf/2026-15666.pdf

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing final regulations to revise how an employee may appeal a furlough of more than 30 days, separation, or demotion by a reduction-in-force (RIF) action. OPM will replace the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) as the adjudicative agency for such appeals. The rule establishes a uniform, record-based OPM appeal process; clarifies the appellant's burden; requires production of the complete agency record; preserves collateral statutory remedies; and applies prospectively to improve timeliness, consistency, and cost-effectiveness while maintaining administrative review.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

  3071      Under the prior regulatory framework, a RIF appeal filed with MSPB 
  3072  could proceed through multiple adjudicative stages. First, the appeal 
  3073  was assigned to an MSPB administrative judge, who possessed broad 
  3074  authority to conduct the proceeding, including authority to rule on

  3082  scheduling, presentation of testimony and evidence, a hearing record or

Topics:            Administrative practice and procedure, Emergency preparedness, Government employees, Health facilities, Health insurance, Health professions, Hospitals, Hostages, Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon, Military personnel, Reporting and recordkeeping requirements, Retirement, Students, Wages, Weather
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/19/2026-21316/managing-senior-professional-performance
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-19/pdf/2026-21316.pdf

Abstract:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) are issuing a final rule to strengthen the performance appraisal of senior-level (SL) and scientific or professional (ST) employees, collectively referred to as "senior professionals." This final rule establishes a new subpart dedicated exclusively to senior professional performance appraisal that aligns more closely with Senior Executive Service (SES) performance appraisal regulations. The rule also eliminates senior professional appraisal programs, removes the prohibition of a standardized distribution of performance rating levels, and enhances oversight of the appraisal process.

| Bianchi | 5 + 0 + 3 | **8** | 5 | **13** | I |
| Castillo | 7 + 5 + 5 | **17** | 0 | **17** | I |
| Dalton | Two actual values 7 and 0; missing-rating proxy = (7 + 0)/2 = 3.5; total = 7 + 0 + 3.5 | **10.5** | 3 | **13.5** | I |
| Eze | 5 + 5 + 5 | **15** | 0 | **15** | II |
| Fontaine | One actual Level 4: 5 × 3 | **15** | 0 | **15** | I |

Dalton's proxy follows §351.503(f)(2); Fontaine's multiplication follows (f)(3). Castillo is **not** a RIF preference eligible: his length-of-service retirement after 22 active years satisfies none of §351.504(b)(1)–(3), and his officer rank does not supply an alternative entitlement under (b)(4). Eze's four-year term appointment is not the excluded temporary appointment of one year or less; after probation he falls in subgroup II under §351.502(a)(3).

(b) Highest to lowest:

1. **Abbott—17, I**
2. **Castillo—17, I**
3. **Fontaine—15, I**
4. **Eze—15, II**
5. **Dalton—13.5, I**
6. **Bianchi—13, I**

Abbott and Castillo have equal totals and tenure subgroups, so Abbott's **May 1, 2003** SCD precedes Castillo's **August 1, 2012** SCD. Fontaine beats Eze at 15 because subgroup I precedes II; Eze's earlier SCD never becomes the deciding factor. Those are the tie-breakers in §351.501(c). **Bianchi and Dalton are released from the competitive level.** Release is not necessarily separation if assignment rights exist; none are supplied here.

(c) Under the earlier system **Bianchi would have stood above Abbott**. Both were career employees in former tenure group I, but Bianchi's AD veterans' preference subgroup preceded Abbott's B subgroup before performance-adjusted service dates were compared. This is the earlier system as described by OPM's preamble, not a reconstruction of unprinted former CFR text.

(d) Having received a specific notice, Bianchi may inspect the **complete retention register and related completed records used in her RIF action**, including all employees' names and the retention information needed to examine the scoring and relative ranking. Relevant registers affecting competitive-level composition or assignment rights are also reviewable; her representative may inspect on her behalf. Q4.answer:
(a) With no cutoff, the lookback ends at **September 3, 2026**, and begins four years earlier. Farah's three most recent qualifying ratings are August 10, 2026, Level 5; November 14, 2025, Level 3; and November 15, 2024, Level 3. Credit = **7 + 3 + 3 = 13** (§351.503(a), (c)(1)).

(b) September 3 − 45 calendar days = **July 20, 2026**: July 21–31 contributes 11 days, August 31 days, and September 1–3 three days; **11 + 31 + 3 = 45**. The four-year period now ends at July 20, not September 3. August 10's rating is excluded. The three most recent are November 2025 Level 3, November 2024 Level 3, and November 2023 Level 4: **3 + 3 + 5 = 11** (§351.503(c)(2)).

(c) **July 15 issuance alone is insufficient.** Section 351.503(c)(3) also requires the completed rating to be ‘on record,’ expressly meaning available for use by the office establishing retention registers. If August 15 was its first availability to that office, it **cannot** be used under the July 20 cutoff. Conversely, late entry in a particular computer system does not itself disqualify a rating that was already otherwise available to the responsible office by July 20; availability, not a named system's entry date, is the regulatory test.

(d) Gina's August 15, 2022 rating is outside the four years preceding September 3, 2026. Her actual values are 5 for Level 4 and 3 for Level 3. Missing-rating proxy = **(5 + 3)/2 = 4**. Performance credit = **5 + 3 + 4 = 12**, under §351.503(f)(2).

(e) Hank receives **modal-rating-based credit** for the summary-level pattern applicable to his official position at the time of the RIF, under §351.503(f)(1). His former organization's ratings are not usable when the agency has not determined them equivalent under §351.503(b)(3). He does **not** automatically receive a presumed Level 3. The facts do not establish a numerical modal-rating credit.

(a) Jordan's Level 2 current annual rating satisfies §351.701(a). A one-grade progression makes the ordinary three-grade lower limit **GS-10**: 13 − 3 = 10.

| Position | Assignment right? | Reason |

| **1. Ellis, GS-12** | **Yes; this is the required offer** | Qualified, lower-standing holder, same tenure group, area and schedule; least reduction in representative rate. |
| **2. Frank, GS-11** | Yes, but not the required offer while position 1 is available | Within two grades and otherwise eligible; greater pay reduction than GS-12. |
| **3. Gale, GS-10** | Yes, but not the required offer while position 1 is available | Exactly three grades lower; otherwise eligible. |
| **4. Hana, GS-9** | **No** | Four grades below GS-13, beyond the ordinary limit. |
| **5. Ito, GS-12** | **No** | The holder has higher retention standing. |
| **6. Kim, part-time GS-12** | **No** | Different type of work schedule. |
| **7. Lund, GS-12 elsewhere** | **No** | Outside Jordan's competitive area. |

These are §351.701(a), (b), and (d) requirements; the agency must select an eligible offer requiring no reduction or the least possible reduction in representative rate.

(b) For a preference eligible with a compensable service-connected disability of 30 percent or more, §351.701(b)(2) expands the lower limit to **five grades**: 13 − 5 = **GS-8**. **Position 4 becomes reachable**. Position 1 remains the required offer, and positions 5–7 remain unavailable for their independent defects.

(c) With a current annual **Level 1**, Jordan does not meet §351.701(a)'s minimum Level 2 requirement and has **no mandatory assignment right under that section**.

(d) Section 351.701 does not give the excepted-service employees these mandatory rights. Under §351.705(a), the agency **may adopt** equivalent assignment rights for competing excepted-service employees to positions **under the same appointing authority**. If it has adopted them and that condition is satisfied, the same position-by-position analysis applies; otherwise the mandatory offer cannot be inferred.

The operative question is lower **retention standing**, not whether the incumbent's current rating is higher. Q7.answer:
(a) **MSPB** is the intended forum for the August 31-notice/October 30-separation case. The controlling OPM transition is based on **notice issuance before September 2**, not separation after that date. The principal documents are:

The appeals proposal, **2026-02576**, is background only, not governing authority.

(b) The October 19 notice invokes the **OPM appeal process**. Morgan or her authorized representative must use the electronic filing system identified on OPM's website, absent an approved good-cause exception (§351.902(a), (c)).

Counting from the December 18, 2026 separation:

- December 19 is day 1.
- December 19–31 = **13 days**.
- January 1–17 = **17 more days**; day 30 is **Sunday, January 17, 2027**.
- Monday, January 18 is the Martin Luther King Jr. federal holiday, the third Monday in January.
- The first following workday is **Tuesday, January 19, 2027**.

The timely electronic-filing deadline is therefore **11:59 p.m. Eastern Time, January 19, 2027**, under §351.902(b)–(b)(1).

(c) By a **preponderance of the evidence**, Morgan must prove: timely written appeal; OPM jurisdiction; agency noncompliance with an applicable RIF statute or OPM regulation; and resulting prejudice—causing the appealed action or loss of a materially more favorable outcome (§351.901(b)). She has **no automatic hearing entitlement**. Review is on the developed written record unless OPM finds a hearing necessary and efficient, including an inadequately developed material fact or material witness-credibility dispute (§351.905(c)).

(d) The adopted §351.901(c)(2) **bars** raising the RIF action, or matters relating to its appeal, under a negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. The preamble nevertheless says OPM is **not automatically invalidating existing CBAs mid-term**; the rule limits inconsistent bargaining when agreements are renegotiated, and questions about particular existing agreements remain for the appropriate chapter 71 forum. That qualification is not an express grandfather clause in the regulatory text.

(e) **Not under this regulatory RIF appeal process.** Section 351.901(c)(4) says a party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under subpart I; §351.909(e) denies further appeal of a final OPM decision. The preamble distinguishes independent collateral statutory claims and their own judicial remedies from review of the OPM RIF decision itself.

(f) **Yes, conditionally, even though she did not initially appeal the RIF.** Corrected §351.902(b)(3) permits a later RIF appeal if the collateral complaint was timely filed before expiration of the original RIF filing period, its decision is final beyond further administrative review, and OPM determines that it materially affects part 351 rights. A corrected rating changing retention standing fits the described type of material effect.

If March 10, 2027 is that finality date: March 11–31 = **21 days**; April 1–9 = **9 days**; total **30**. The resulting deadline is **Friday, April 9, 2027, 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time**.

(g) There is **no separately codified applicability paragraph** deciding between (a) and (b). The exact front-matter provision is **2026-15666, DATES, 91 FR 49230**: the rule applies only where the agency issues the employee a specific notice under §351.802 on or after September 2, 2026. **IV.C.1, 91 FR 49248**, expressly states that an earlier-issued notice remains with MSPB and expressly says the applicability provision is in the preamble, not a separate note in §351.901.

Q8.answer:
(a) **As of November 14**, §351.806's existing rule is described by OPM as keeping the employee in duty status **‘when possible.’** Its longstanding emergency provision permits annual leave with or without consent, leave without pay with consent, or a nonpay status without consent when the agency lacks work or funds in an emergency. OPM identifies the emergency language as unchanged when republishing it in the new rule.

The adopted but not yet effective replacement is **2026-21320**, effective **November 18, 2026**:

- **(a):** under ordinary circumstances the employee remains in duty status.
- **(b):** the agency may place the employee on administrative leave for all or part of the notice period when appropriate and consistent with part 630, subpart N.
- **(c):** the emergency lack-of-work-or-funds provision described above.

Thus the October 26 placements cannot be justified by treating the November 18 amendment as already operative.

(b) Under the adopted text, **employee consent is not a condition** of RIF notice-period administrative leave. Companion **§630.1403(c)(10)** authorizes leave between receipt of the notice and RIF separation when the agency determines it is in the Government's best interests. Neither that paragraph nor §351.806(b) establishes a separate numerical maximum; the leave may cover **all or part of the actual notice period**, subject to applicable part 630 requirements and policies. It is not authority to continue notice-period leave beyond separation.

The preamble explains that the 10-workday limit concerns investigative administrative leave. The express Governmentwide-limit language attached to deferred-resignation and settlement leave in §630.1403(c)(9) and (11), including the preamble's discussion of a 12-week policy, should not be silently inserted into the differently worded RIF paragraph (c)(10).

(c) OPM says **existing policy guidance already allowed this use**: section D.1.b of its July 30, 2025 memorandum, *Template for Agency Administrative Leave Policies*, CPM 2025-12, allowed administrative leave between receipt of an involuntary-separation notice and its effective date. The proposal also explained that keeping an employee on duty might jeopardize Government interests. These are preamble accounts of existing guidance, not an assertion that the November amendment was effective in October.

(d) **No.** OPM expressly says these amendments address paid nonduty status only and do not alter substantive or procedural RIF requirements. They do not bypass competition, retention registers or appeal rights. Retention standing remains governed by §351.507, including receipt-based fixation and correction of errors; notice and appeal requirements continue independently.
